abstract.1: This review addresses the pathophysiology and treatment of hemorrhagic shock - a condition produced by rapid and significant loss of intravascular volume, which may lead sequentially to hemodynamic instability, decreases in oxygen delivery, decreased tissue perfusion, cellular hypoxia, organ damage, and death.
abstract.2: Hemorrhagic shock can be rapidly fatal.
abstract.3: The primary goals are to stop the bleeding and to restore circulating blood volume.
abstract.4: Resuscitation may well depend on the estimated severity of hemorrhage.
abstract.5: It now appears that patients with moderate hypotension from bleeding may benefit by delaying massive fluid resuscitation until they reach a definitive care facility.
abstract.6: On the other hand, the use of intravenous fluids, crystalloids or colloids, and blood products can be life saving in those patients who are in severe hemorrhagic shock.
abstract.7: The optimal method of resuscitation has not been clearly established.
abstract.8: A hemoglobin level of 7-8 g/dl appears to be an appropriate threshold for transfusion in critically ill patients with no evidence of tissue hypoxia.
abstract.9: However, maintaining a higher hemoglobin level of 10 g/dl is a reasonable goal in actively bleeding patients, the elderly, or individuals who are at risk for myocardial infarction.
abstract.10: Moreover, hemoglobin concentration should not be the only therapeutic guide in actively bleeding patients.
abstract.11: Instead, therapy should be aimed at restoring intravascular volume and adequate hemodynamic parameters.

adaptation1.11: Instead, therapy should be aimed at restoring blood volume, blood pressure, and heart rate.

25284231.Title: The ATLS(®) classification of hypovolaemic shock: a well established teaching tool on the edge?

abstract.1: Uncontrolled bleeding is the leading cause of shock in trauma patients and delays in recognition and treatment have been linked to adverse outcomes.
abstract.2: For prompt detection and management of hypovolaemic shock, ATLS(®) suggests four shock classes based upon vital signs and an estimated blood loss in percent.
abstract.3: Although this classification has been widely implemented over the past decades, there is still no clear prospective evidence to fully support this classification.
abstract.4: In contrast, it has recently been shown that this classification may be associated with substantial deficits.
abstract.5: A retrospective analysis of data derived from the TraumaRegister DGU(®) indicated that only 9.3% of all trauma patients could be allocated into one of the ATLS(®) shock classes when a combination of the three vital signs heart rate, systolic blood pressure and Glasgow Coma Scale was assessed.
abstract.6: Consequently, more than 90% of all trauma patients could not be classified according to the ATLS(®) classification of hypovolaemic shock.
abstract.7: Further analyses including also data from the UK-based TARN registry suggested that ATLS(®) may overestimate the degree of tachycardia associated with hypotension and underestimate mental disability in the presence of hypovolaemic shock.
abstract.8: This finding was independent from pre-hospital treatment as well as from the presence or absence of a severe traumatic brain injury.
abstract.9: Interestingly, even the underlying trauma mechanism (blunt or penetrating) had no influence on the number of patients who could be allocated adequately.
abstract.10: Considering these potential deficits associated with the ATLS(®) classification of hypovolaemic shock, an online survey among 383 European ATLS(®) course instructors and directors was performed to assess the actual appreciation and confidence in this tool during daily clinical trauma care.
abstract.11: Interestingly, less than half (48%) of all respondents declared that they would assess a potential circulatory depletion within the primary survey according to the ATLS(®) classification of hypovolaemic shock.
abstract.12: Based on these observations, a critical reappraisal of the current ATLS(®) classification of hypovolaemic seems warranted.

adaptation1.2: For quick detection and management of hypovolemic shock, ATLS(®) suggests four shock classes. These classes are based upon vital signs and an estimated blood loss in percent. Hypovolemic shock is due to volume loss with blood vessels or blood vascular system.

adaptation1.4: In contrast, it has recently been shown that this classification may be associated with substantial deficits.

adaptation1.6: Because of this, more than 90% of all trauma patients could not be classified according to the ATLS(®) classification of hypovolemic shock.
adaptation1.7: Further review included data from the UK-based TARN registry. This evaluation suggested that ATLS(®) may overestimate the degree of tachycardia (high heart rate) associated with low blood pressure and underestimate mental disability in the presence of hypovolemic shock.
adaptation1.8: This finding was independent from pre-hospital treatment and from the presence or absence of a severe traumatic brain injury.
adaptation1.9: The underlying trauma mechanism, or what caused the injury, had no influence on the number of patients who could be categorized.

The survey assessed 383 European ATLS(®) course instructors and directors. The survey was completed to assess the understanding and confidence in this tool during daily clinical trauma care.
adaptation1.11: Less than half of all respondents declared that they would assess a potential circulatory depletion within the primary survey according to the ATLS(®) classification of hypovolemic shock.
adaptation1.12: Based on these observations, a critical reappraisal (revision) of the current ATLS(®) classification of hypovolemic is needed.

25565640.Title: Individual-Specific, Beat-to-beat Trending of Significant Human Blood Loss: The Compensatory Reserve

abstract.1: Current monitoring technologies are unable to detect early, compensatory changes that are associated with significant blood loss.
abstract.2: We previously introduced a novel algorithm to calculate the Compensatory Reserve Index (CRI) based on the analysis of arterial waveform features obtained from photoplethysmogram recordings.
abstract.3: In the present study, we hypothesized that the CRI would provide greater sensitivity and specificity to detect blood loss compared with traditional vital signs and other hemodynamic measures.
abstract.4: Continuous noninvasive vital sign waveform data, including CRI, photoplethysmogram, heart rate, blood pressures, SpO2, cardiac output, and stroke volume, were analyzed from 20 subjects before, during, and after an average controlled voluntary hemorrhage of ∼1.2 L of blood.
abstract.5: Compensatory Reserve Index decreased by 33% in a linear fashion across progressive blood volume loss, with no clinically significant alterations in vital signs.
abstract.6: The receiver operating characteristic area under the curve for the CRI was 0.90, with a sensitivity of 0.80 and specificity of 0.76.
abstract.7: In comparison, blood pressures, heart rate, SpO2, cardiac output, and stroke volume had significantly lower receiver operating characteristic area under the curve values and specificities for detecting the same volume of blood loss.
abstract.8: Consistent with our hypothesis, CRI detected blood loss and restoration with significantly greater specificity than did other traditional physiologic measures.
abstract.9: Single measurement of CRI may enable more accurate triage, whereas CRI monitoring may allow for earlier detection of casualty deterioration.

adaptation1.1: Current monitoring technologies are unable to detect early changes associated with significant blood loss.
adaptation1.2: A novel model to calculate the Compensatory Reserve Index (CRI) was previously introduced by the authors in a secondary study. CRI measures physiological reserve, or how an organ responds to stress, which can be used as an indicator of how a patient will respond to intensive care.
adaptation1.3: In the present study, the authors hypothesized that the CRI would provide greater sensitivity and specificity to detect blood loss compared to traditional methods.
adaptation1.4: Vital signs were analyzed from 20 subjects before, during, and after an average controlled voluntary hemorrhage (excessive blood loss) of ∼1.2 L of blood.
adaptation1.5: CRI decreased across progressive blood volume loss, with no clinically significant alterations in vital signs.
adaptation1.6: Statistical analysis of CRI showed high confidence in the ability of the test to produce accurate results.
adaptation1.7: In contrast, blood pressures, heart rate, SpO2, cardiac output, and stroke volume had significantly lower confidence  for detection and specificity rates.
adaptation1.8: CRI detected blood loss and restoration with greater specificity than did other traditional measures.
adaptation1.9: Single measurement of CRI may enable more accurate assessment of health emergencies. CRI monitoring may allow for earlier detection of declining health.

adaptation2.1: Current monitoring technologies cannot detect early, counterbalancing changes associated with significant blood loss.
adaptation2.2: We previously showed a new mathematical equation to calculate the counterbalancing blood flow mechanics or Compensatory Reserve Index (CRI) based on analysis of blood vessel wave patterns from blood flow recordings.
adaptation2.3: In the present study, we theorized that CRI would give better accuracy to detect blood loss compared to standard vital signs and other blood flow measures.
adaptation2.4: We analyzed 20 subjects before, during, and after a regular, controlled voluntary blood loss of 1.2 liters for continuous non-surgical vital sign wave data, including CRI, recordings, heart rate, blood pressure, oxygen levels, blood flow output, and blood volume.
adaptation2.5: CRI decreased by 33% in a linear trend across increasing blood volume loss, with no changes in vital signs.
adaptation2.6: CRI had high accuracy for detecting blood volume loss.
adaptation2.7: In comparison, blood pressure, heart rate, oxygen levels, blood flow output and blood volume had less accuracy for detecting the same amount of blood loss.
adaptation2.8: Consistent with out theory, CRI detected blood loss and restoration better than other traditional body measures.
adaptation2.9: Single measurement of CRI may enable better identification, while CRI monitoring may allow earlier detection of patient status trending towards death.

28346013.Title: The physiology of blood loss and shock: New insights from a human laboratory model of hemorrhage

abstract.1: Development of a human model of hemorrhage has provided a unique opportunity to investigate the underlying physiology that defines the individual capacity to avoid the life-threatening clinical condition of inadequate tissue oxygenation known as “shock.”
abstract.2: The experimental approach of progressively reducing central blood volume to the point of hemodynamic decompensation with the use of lower body negative pressure has revealed stark distinctions in the physiological compensatory responses between individuals with high compared with low tolerances to blood loss.
abstract.3: High tolerance to hemorrhage is defined by a capacity to maintain systemic perfusion pressure and reduce the rate of cerebral hypoperfusion by: (1) protecting cardiac output with greater elevations in heart rate associated with greater cardiac vagal withdrawal and sympathetically mediated adrenergic stimulation; (2) greater increases in systemic peripheral vascular resistance associated with higher sympathetic nerve activation and levels of circulating vasopressor endocrine responses; (3) alternating blood flow between the brain and peripheral tissue with greater sympathetically mediated oscillatory patterns of systemic pressure and flow; and (4) enhancing cardiac filling and cerebral perfusion pressure gradient by optimizing the respiratory pump.
abstract.4: When the capacity for these compensatory responses is exhausted, an active vasodilation drops resistance to blood flow allowing for increased perfusion of peripheral tissue.
abstract.5: When cardiac filling is no longer adequate to maintain systemic pressure and flow, a reflex-mediated pronounced bradycardia leads to the initiation of decompensatory shock.

adaptation1.1: A human model of hemorrhage (excessive bleeding) provides the opportunity to investigate the underlying mechanisms that can help someone avoid the life-threatening condition of inadequate tissue oxygenation known as "shock."
adaptation1.2: This is completed by experimentally reducing central blood volume. Blood volume is progressively decreased to the point of critically low blood pressure. This test approach has shown differences in the bodily responses between individuals with high tolerances versus low tolerances to blood loss.
adaptation1.3: High tolerance to hemorrhage is defined by maintaining body wide blood flow pressure and prevent decreased brain blood pressure. This is done by one of four ways.  First, by protecting cardiac output with greater elevations in heart rate associated with greater cardiac vagal withdrawal and sympathetically mediated adrenergic stimulation. Second, a greater increases in systemic peripheral vascular resistance (blood vessel resistance) associated with higher sympathetic nerve activation (fight-or-flight reaction) and levels of circulating vasopressor endocrine responses (responses from chemical messengers). Third, an alternating blood flow between the brain and peripheral tissue with greater sympathetically mediated oscillatory patterns of systemic pressure and flow. Lastly, by enhancing cardiac filling and cerebral perfusion pressure gradient (pressure driving oxygen to brain tissue) by optimizing the respiratory pump (muscles that help the lung extract and contract).
adaptation1.4: When these compensatory responses are exhausted, an active vasodilation (enlargement of blood vessels) drops resistance to blood flow allowing for increased perfusion of peripheral tissue.
adaptation1.5: When the body no is longer able to maintain systemic pressure and flow, a decreased heart rate leads to the initiation of decompensatory shock.

abstract.1: Etiology: Though most commonly thought of in the setting of trauma, there are numerous causes of hemorrhagic shock that span many systems.
abstract.2: Blunt or penetrating trauma is the most common cause, followed by upper and lower gastrointestinal sources.
abstract.3: Obstetrical, vascular, iatrogenic, and even urological sources have all been described.
abstract.4: Bleeding may be either external or internal.
abstract.5: A substantial amount of blood loss to the point of hemodynamic compromise may occur in the chest, abdomen, or retroperitoneum.
abstract.6: The thigh itself can hold up to 1 L to 2 L of blood.
abstract.7: Pathophysiology: Hemorrhagic shock is due to the depletion of intravascular volume through blood loss to the point of being unable to match the tissues demand for oxygen.
abstract.8: As a result, mitochondria are no longer able to sustain aerobic metabolism for the production of oxygen and switch to the less efficient anaerobic metabolism to meet the cellular demand for adenosine triphosphate.
abstract.9: In the latter process, pyruvate is produced and converted to lactic acid to regenerate nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+) to maintain some degree of cellular respiration in the absence of oxygen.
abstract.10: The body compensates for volume loss by increasing heart rate and contractility, followed by baroreceptor activation resulting in sympathetic nervous system activation and peripheral vasoconstriction.
abstract.11: Typically, there is a slight increase in the diastolic blood pressure with narrowing of the pulse pressure.
abstract.12: As diastolic ventricular filling continues to decline and cardiac output decreases, systolic blood pressure drops.
abstract.13: Due to sympathetic nervous system activation, blood is diverted away from noncritical organs and tissues to preserve blood supply to vital organs such as the heart and brain.
abstract.14: While prolonging heart and brain function, this also leads to other tissues being further deprived of oxygen causing more lactic acid production and worsening acidosis.
abstract.15: This worsening acidosis along with hypoxemia, if left uncorrected, eventually causes the loss of peripheral vasoconstriction, worsening hemodynamic compromise, and death.
abstract.16: The body’s compensation varies by cardiopulmonary comorbidities, age, and vasoactive medications.
abstract.17: Due to these factors, heart rate and blood pressure responses are extremely variable and, therefore, cannot be relied upon as the sole means of diagnosis.

adaptation1.1: Though most found in trauma cases, there are numerous causes of hemorrhagic (excessive bleeding) shock stemming from various organ systems.
adaptation1.2: Blunt or penetrating trauma (injury) is the most common cause. Additional causes include upper and lower gastrointestinal (stomach) sources.
adaptation1.3: Obstetrical (related to childbirth), vascular (related to blood vessels), iatrogenic (illness caused by medical exams), and even urological (related to the urinary tract) sources have all been described.
adaptation1.4: Bleeding may be either external or internal.
adaptation1.5: A substantial amount of blood loss, to the point of dysregulated (incorrect) blood flow, may occur in the chest, abdomen, or in the retroperitoneum. The retroperitoneum is area in the back of the abdomen not covered by the peritoneum.
adaptation1.6: The thigh can hold up to 1 L to 2 L of blood.
adaptation1.7: Hemorrhagic shock is caused by the blood loss in vessels to the point of being unable to match the tissues demand for oxygen.
adaptation1.8: As a result, mitochondria (cell part responsible for making chemical energy) are unable to sustain metabolisms needed for oxygen production. Mitochondria switch to the less efficient metabolism to meet cell demand.
adaptation1.9: Pyruvate, a chemical product of energy production, is produced and converted to maintain some cellular respiration (energy creation) in the absence of oxygen.
adaptation1.10: The body compensates for volume loss by increasing heart rate and contractions. These alterations are followed by baroreceptor activation, which is the increased activity of receptors to regulate blood pressure. The resulting endpoints are sympathetic nervous system activation (fight-or-flight activation) and constriction of blood vessels. The sympathetic nervous system is responsible for heart rate, blood pressure, breathing rate, and pupil size.
adaptation1.11: There is normally a slight increase in the diastolic blood pressure (when the heart is relaxed) with decreased pulse pressure.
adaptation1.12: As the rate in which the heart fills with blood declines and cardiac output decreases, systolic blood pressure (heart is contracting) drops.
adaptation1.13: Due to sympathetic nervous system activation, blood is moved away from noncritical organs and tissues. This is done to preserve blood supply to vital organs like the heart and brain.
adaptation1.14: While prolonging heart and brain function, this blood movement leads to other tissues being deprived of oxygen. This deprivation can cause more lactic acid production and a build up of acid in the blood.
adaptation1.15: This acid build up along with low blood oxygen, if left uncorrected, eventually causes the loss of peripheral vasoconstriction (narrowed blood vessels), decreased blood flow, and death.
adaptation1.16: How the body handles this varies by accompanying heart and lung diseases, age, and blood pressure medications.
adaptation1.17: Due to these factors, heart rate and blood pressure responses are extremely different between patients. Therefore, heart rate and blood pressure cannot be the sole reasons of diagnosis.

29329171.Title: Nonhuman Primate (Rhesus Macaque) Models of Severe Pressure-Targeted Hemorrhagic and Polytraumatic Hemorrhagic Shock

abstract.1: Background: We endeavored to develop clinically translatable nonhuman primate (NHP) models of severe polytraumatic hemorrhagic shock.
abstract.2: Methods: NHPs were randomized into five severe pressure-targeted hemorrhagic shock (PTHS) ± additional injuries scenarios: 30-min PTHS (PTHS-30), 60-min PTHS (PTHS-60), PTHS-60 + soft tissue injury (PTHS-60+ST), PTHS-60+ ST + femur fracture (PTHS-60+ST+FF), and decompensated PTHS+ST+FF (PTHS-D).
abstract.3: Physiologic parameters were recorded and blood samples collected at five time points with animal observation through T = 24 h.
abstract.4: Results presented as mean ± SEM; statistics: log transformation followed by two-way ANOVA with Bonferroni multiple comparisons, Wilcoxon nonparametric test for comparisons, and the Friedmans' one-way ANOVA; significance: P < 0.05.
abstract.5: Results: Percent blood loss was 40% ± 2, 59% ± 3, 52% ± 3, 49% ± 2, and 54% ± 2 for PTHS-30, PTHS-60, PTHS-60+ST, PTHS-60+ST+FF, and PTHS-D, respectively.
abstract.6: All animals survived to T = 24 h except one in each of the PTHS-60 and PTHS-60+ST+FF groups and seven in the PTHS-D group.
abstract.7: Physiologic, coagulation, and inflammatory parameters demonstrated increasing derangements with increasing model severity.
abstract.8: Conclusion: NHPs exhibit a high degree of resilience to hemorrhagic shock and polytrauma as evidenced by moderate perturbations in metabolic, coagulation, and immunologic outcomes with up to 60 min of profound hypotension regardless of injury pattern.
abstract.9: Extending the duration of PTHS to the point of decompensation in combination with polytraumatic injury, evoked derangements consistent with those observed in severely injured trauma patients which would require ICU care.
abstract.10: Thus, we have successfully established a clinically translatable NHP trauma model for use in testing therapeutic interventions to trauma.

adaptation1.1: This study aimed to develop nonhuman primate (monkey) (NHP) models of severe polytraumatic (many-injury) hemorrhagic (excessive bleeding) shock that are applicable to human health settings.
adaptation1.2: NHPs were placed into five pressure-targeted hemorrhagic shock (PTHS) scenarios. The scenarios were as follows: 30-min PTHS (PTHS-30), 60-min PTHS (PTHS-60), PTHS-60 + soft tissue injury (PTHS-60+ST), PTHS-60+ ST + femur (leg) fracture (PTHS-60+ST+FF), and decompensated PTHS+ST+FF (PTHS-D).
adaptation1.3: Physiologic parameters were recorded. Blood samples were collected at five time points with animal observation through 24 hours.
adaptation1.5: Blood loss percentages were  40%, 59%, 52%, 49%, and 54% for PTHS-30, PTHS-60, PTHS-60+ST, PTHS-60+ST+FF, and PTHS-D, respectively.
adaptation1.6: All animals survived till the end of the study except one in the PTHS-60 and PTHS-60+ST+FF groups. Seven did not survive till the end of the study in the PTHS-D group.
adaptation1.7: Physiologic (overall health), coagulation (blood clotting), and inflammatory (infection-fighting) parameters showed increased disturbance with increasing model severity.
adaptation1.8: NHPs show a high degree of resilience to hemorrhagic shock and polytrauma (more than one injury). This was shown by moderate disturbances in metabolic, coagulation, and immunologic outcomes with low blood pressure in all injury groups.
adaptation1.9: Increasing PTHS duration to the point of organ failure with polytraumatic injury, evoked (led to) disturbances consistent with those observed in severely injured trauma patients requiring ICU care.
adaptation1.10: This study has successfully established a clinically translatable NHP trauma model for use in testing therapeutic interventions to trauma.

abstract.1: The term "shock" refers to a life-threatening circulatory failure caused by an imbalance between the supply and demand of cellular oxygen.
abstract.2: Hypovolemic shock is characterized by a reduction of intravascular volume and a subsequent reduction in preload.
abstract.3: The body compensates the loss of volume by increasing the stroke volume, heart frequency, oxygen extraction rate, and later by an increased concentration of 2,3-diphosphoglycerate with a rightward shift of the oxygen dissociation curve.
abstract.4: Hypovolemic hemorrhagic shock impairs the macrocirculation and microcirculation and therefore affects many organ systems (e.g. kidneys, endocrine system and endothelium).
abstract.5: For further identification of a state of shock caused by bleeding, vital functions, coagulation tests and hematopoietic procedures are implemented.
abstract.6: Every hospital should be in possession of a specific protocol for massive transfusions.
abstract.7: The differentiated systemic treatment of bleeding consists of maintenance of an adequate homeostasis and the administration of blood products and coagulation factors.

adaptation1.1: "Shock" refers to a life-threatening circulatory failure. Shock is caused by an imbalance between the supply and demand of oxygen within cells.
adaptation1.2: Hypovolemic shock is characterized by a decreased volume in blood vessels and a subsequent reduction in preload (volume of blood within the heart when its relaxed).
adaptation1.3: The body compensates the volume loss by increasing stroke volume, heart frequency, and oxygen extraction rate. Following these steps, the body will then increase 2,3-diphosphoglycerate (a chemical that controls oxygen movement) to increase available oxygen.
adaptation1.4: Hypovolemic shock is due to volume loss with blood vessels or blood vascular system. Hypovolemic hemorrhagic shock impairs blood circulation. Because of this, this type of shock affects many organ systems.
adaptation1.5: Vital functions, coagulation (blood) tests, and hematopoietic (blood cell creation) procedures are used to identify a state of shock caused by bleeding.
adaptation1.6: Every hospital should have a specific protocol for massive transfusions (transfers).
adaptation1.7: Treatment of bleeding within the body consists of homeostasis (bodily equilibrium) maintenance and administration (use) of blood products and blood clothing (scabbing) medications.

adaptation2.1: The term "shock" refers to a life-threatening blood-flow-related failure caused by an imbalance between supply and demand of oxygen for cells.
adaptation2.2: Hypovolemic shock is due to a reduced amount of blood in vessels and subsequently reduced amount of blood and oxygen to pump.
adaptation2.3: The body compensates for the loss of volume by increasing blood volume per pump, heart rate, oxygen extraction rate, and increasing the amount of a specific molecule that increases oxygen release.
adaptation2.4: Hypovolemic shock from blood loss impairs blood circulation and affects many organs (e.g., kidneys, hormonal system, and blood vessel tubing).
adaptation2.5: For futher identification of shock due to bleeding, vital functions, blood clotting or thickening tests and procedures assessing blood cell development are used.
adaptation2.6: Every hospital should have a specific guideline for massive transfusions or transfers.
adaptation2.7: The personalized full-body treatment of bleeding includes maintaing a proper balance in the body and administering blood substances and factors for blood clotting.

30068251.Title: Unmasking the Hypovolemic Shock Continuum: The Compensatory Reserve

abstract.1: Hypovolemic shock exists as a spectrum, with its early stages characterized by subtle pathophysiologic tissue insults and its late stages defined by multi-system organ dysfunction.
abstract.2: The importance of timely detection of shock is well known, as early interventions improve mortality, while delays render these same interventions ineffective.
abstract.3: However, detection is limited by the monitors, parameters, and vital signs that are traditionally used in the intensive care unit (ICU).
abstract.4: Many parameters change minimally during the early stages, and when they finally become abnormal, hypovolemic shock has already occurred.
abstract.5: The compensatory reserve (CR) is a parameter that represents a new paradigm for assessing physiologic status, as it comprises the sum total of compensatory mechanisms that maintain adequate perfusion to vital organs during hypovolemia.
abstract.6: When these mechanisms are overwhelmed, hemodynamic instability and circulatory collapse will follow.
abstract.7: Previous studies involving CR measurements demonstrated their utility in detecting central blood volume loss before hemodynamic parameters and vital signs changed.
abstract.8: Measurements of the CR have also been used in clinical studies involving patients with traumatic injuries or bleeding, and the results from these studies have been promising.
abstract.9: Moreover, these measurements can be made at the bedside, and they provide a real-time assessment of hemodynamic stability.
abstract.10: Given the need for rapid diagnostics when treating critically ill patients, CR measurements would complement parameters that are currently being used.
abstract.11: Consequently, the purpose of this article is to introduce a conceptual framework where the CR represents a new approach to monitoring critically ill patients.
abstract.12: Within this framework, we present evidence to support the notion that the use of the CR could potentially improve the outcomes of ICU patients by alerting intensivists to impending hypovolemic shock before its onset.

adaptation1.1: Hypovolemic shock is a spectrum of reactions. In the early stages of hypovolemic shock, there is subtle pathophysiologic tissue insults. In the late stages of hypovolemic shock, there is multi-system organ dysfunction. Hypovolemic shock is due to volume loss with blood vessels or blood vascular system.
adaptation1.2: Timely detection of shock is important. Early interventions (treatments) decrease the chance of death. Intervention delays can make the same interventions ineffective.
adaptation1.3: Detection can be limited by monitoring, parameters, and vital signs that are used in the intensive care unit (ICU).
adaptation1.4: Most parameters barely change during the early stages. When the signs finally become abnormal, hypovolemic shock has already occurred.
adaptation1.5: The compensatory reserve (CR) is a parameter. It is a new model for assessing body function. CR represents all of the mechanisms or ways the body compensates for internal conditions that dysregulate blood flow to vital organs during hypovolemia.
adaptation1.6: When these mechanisms are overwhelmed, unstable blood pressure, and circulatory failure will follow.
adaptation1.7: Previous studies involving CR measurements have shown its use in detecting central blood volume loss before blood pressure parameters and vital signs changed.
adaptation1.8: CR measurements have also been used in clinical studies involving patients with traumatic injuries or bleeding. The results from these clinical studies have been promising.
adaptation1.9: CR measurements can be made at the bedside. They also provide a real-time assessment of blood flow.
adaptation1.10: There is a need for rapid diagnostics when treating critically ill patients. CR measurements would complement parameters that are currently being used.
adaptation1.11: The aim of this article is to introduce a conceptual framework where the CR represents a new approach to monitoring critically ill patients.
adaptation1.12: Within this framework, the authors present evidence to support the how the use of the CR could potentially improve the outcomes of ICU patients. CR could improve alerting doctors to impending hypovolemic shock before its onset.

30573009.Title: The Nomenclature, Definition and Distinction of Types of Shock

abstract.1: Background: A severe mismatch between the supply and demand of oxygen is the common feature of all types of shock.
abstract.2: We present a newly developed, clinically oriented classification of the various types of shock and their therapeutic implications.
abstract.3: Results: There are only four major categories of shock, each of which is mainly related to one of four organ systems.
abstract.4: Hypovolemic shock relates to the blood and fluids compartment while distributive shock relates to the vascular system; cardiogenic shock arises from primary cardiac dysfunction; and obstructive shock arises from a blockage of the circulation.
abstract.5: Hypovolemic shock is due to intravascular volume loss and is treated by fluid replacement with balanced crystalloids.
abstract.6: Distributive shock, on the other hand, is a state of relative hypovolemia resulting from pathological redistribution of the absolute intravascular volume and is treated with a combination of vasoconstrictors and fluid replacement.
abstract.7: Cardiogenic shock is due to inadequate function of the heart, which shall be treated, depending on the situation, with drugs, surgery, or other interventional procedures.
abstract.8: In obstructive shock, hypoperfusion due to elevated resistance shall be treated with an immediate life-saving intervention.
abstract.9: Pathogenesis and pathophysiology: The characteristic feature of both, hemorrhagic and traumatic hemorrhagic shock is bleeding.
abstract.10: However, differences exist between the two subcategories in terms of the extent of soft tissue damage.
abstract.11: Clinically the most significant cause of hemorrhagic shock is acute bleeding from an isolated injury to a large blood vessel, gastrointestinal bleeding, nontraumatic vascular rupture (e.g., aortic aneurysm), obstetric hemorrhage (e.g., uterine atony), and hemorrhage in the region of the ear, nose, and throat (vascular erosion).
abstract.12: The shock is triggered by the critical drop in circulating blood volume; massive loss of red blood cells intensifies the tissue hypoxia.

adaptation1.1: Inequality between the supply and demand of oxygen is the common feature of shock.
adaptation1.2: This study presents a newly developed, patient-treatment oriented classification of the various types of shock and their therapeutic (helpful) implications.
adaptation1.3: There are four major categories of shock. Each category is mainly related to one of four organ systems.
adaptation1.4: One category, known as hypovolemic shock, relates to the blood and fluids compartment. Distributive shock relates to the vascular system or blood vessels. Cardiogenic shock arises from primary cardiac or heart dysfunction. Obstructive shock arises from a blockage of circulation.
adaptation1.5: Hypovolemic shock is due to volume loss with blood vessels or blood vascular system. This type of shock is treated by replacement with balanced fluids.
adaptation1.6: Distributive shock is a state of low blood plasma. This type of shock comes from volume displacement in blood vessels. It is treated with a combination of vasoconstrictors, drugs that constrict blood vessels to increase blood pressure, and fluid replacement.
adaptation1.7: Cardiogenic shock is caused by inadequate function of the heart, which shall be treated, depending on the situation, with drugs, surgery, or other treatment methods.
adaptation1.8: In obstructive shock, circulatory failure due to increased resistance will be treated with an immediate life-saving intervention.
adaptation1.9: Both hemorrhagic (excessive bleeding from a ruptured blood vessel) and traumatic hemorrhagic (internal bleeding from an injury) shock feature bleeding.
adaptation1.10: However, differences exist between the two subcategories in terms of how much soft tissue damage they create.
adaptation1.11: The most significant cause of hemorrhagic shock is bleeding from an isolated injury to a critical portion of the body. Some of examples of this include injuries to blood vessels or blood within the intestines.
adaptation1.12: The shock is caused by a critical drop in circulating blood volume. Massive loss of red blood cells increases tissue hypoxia (below normal level of oxygen).

31030706.Title: Use of Shock Index to Identify Mild Hemorrhage: An Observational Study in Military Blood Donors

abstract.1: Introduction: Hemorrhage is the leading cause of preventable death in combat, although early recognition of hemorrhage is still challenging on the battlefield.
abstract.2: Hypothesis/Problem: The objective of this study was to describe the shock index (SI) in a healthy military population, and to measure its variation during a controlled blood loss, simulated by blood donation.
abstract.3: Methods: A prospective observational study that enrolled military subjects, volunteers for blood donation, was conducted.
abstract.4: Demographic and clinical information, concerning both the patient and the blood collection, were recorded.
abstract.5: Baseline vital signs were measured, before and after donation, in a 45° supine position.
abstract.6: Statistical analysis was performed after calculation of SI.
abstract.7: Results: A total of 483 participants were included in the study.
abstract.8: The mean blood donation volume was 473mL (SD = 44mL).
abstract.9: The median pre- and post-blood donation SI were significantly different: 0.54 (IQR = 0.48-0.63) and 0.57 (IQR = 0.49-0.66), respectively (P = .002).
abstract.10: Changes in pre-/post-donation blood pressure (BP) and heart rate (HR) also reached statistical difference but represented a clinically poor relevance.
abstract.11: The multivariate analysis showed no significant associations between SI variations and age, sex, body mass index (BMI), sport activities, blood donation volume, and enteral volume replacement (EVR).
abstract.12: Conclusion: In this model of mild hemorrhage, SI exhibited significant variations but failed to reach clinical relevance.
abstract.13: Further studies are needed to prove the benefit of SI calculation as a possible parameter for early recognition of hemorrhage in combat casualties at the point of injury.
